To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
brief bursts of activity self-inhibit the network by activating disynaptic inhibition and that the network synchronizes in response to these bursts.

(1) Brief bursts of action potential firing in neocortical neurons can trigger disynaptic inhibition that is frequency dependent and (2) this inhibition can be summed across multiple synapses and across multiple pyramidal neurons to synchronize the entire microcircuits of neocortical networks.
brief bursts of activity can self-inhibit and synchronize a network of cortical pyramidal cells.

the role of inhibitory circuits in the generation of oscillatory and rhythmic activity, the role of inhibition in the control of the balance between excitation and inhibition in cortical networks and the mechanisms of inhibition in the neocortex.
understanding the mechanisms underlying the generation, propagation and integration of neuronal activity in the mammalian brain.
the development and use of new methods for measuring, modeling, and understanding the structure and function of the human brain.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
brief bursts in the pyramidal network are not only capable of generating a large amount of inhibition, but also that they correlate the pyramidal population.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the neocortical microcircuit is organized as a set of interacting modules, with the inhibitory interneurons acting as a switch to control the flow of information between them.
the neocortex can be viewed as a network of oscillators with a broad distribution of natural frequencies and a wide range of coupling strengths.
the neocortical network is organized in a way that enables brief bursts to spread rapidly and synchronize the network, while at the same time inhibiting itself to prevent runaway activity.
